claims.text: The as-cast, homogenized HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase BCC.
Hf, Zr, Nb, Ta, and Ti have sufficient atomic-size mismatch to contribute to internal stress.
Differential thermal expansion among the constituent elements generates local stress fields.
The local thermal stress fields lower the nucleation barrier for nanoscale clusters.
Thermal-expansion-induced internal stresses drive reversible short-range ordering in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed structural mediator consists of coherent Hf-Zr-rich clusters or incipient HCP nanoprecipitates.
The clusters impede dislocation motion by pinning dislocations.
Formation or dissolution of the clusters changes the alloy's elastic stiffness.
Slow cooling from 900 °C at about 1 °C/min produces a greater retained cluster fraction than quenching at more than 100 °C/s.
Slow-cooled specimens will have about 20% higher room-temperature microhardness than rapidly quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled specimens will exhibit about 15% greater hardening after aging at 600-800 °C than rapidly quenched specimens.
Slow-cooled specimens will show an approximately 5% elastic-modulus drop near 900 K associated with cluster dissolution.
Slow-cooled specimens will have an approximately 30% lower steady-state creep rate at 1250 °C and 100 MPa than rapidly quenched specimens.
Rapidly quenched specimens have minimal cluster volume fraction.
Rapidly quenched specimens exhibit lower hardness, minimal aging hardening, a monotonically increasing modulus, and a higher creep rate relative to slow-cooled specimens.
Clusters do not form appreciably below about 600 °C.
Cluster-driven mechanical effects persist up to about 1250 °C.
The clusters dissolve completely above about 1250 °C.
